body_markdown:
[Flame-resistant clothing](https://unifirst.com/uniforms-workwear/flame-resistant/) (FR clothing) is critical for worker safety in industries exposed to fire and electrical hazards. Whether you’re in construction, manufacturing, or energy sectors, proper FR clothing, including CAT 1, CAT 2, CAT 3, and CAT 4[arc-rated garments](https://unifirst.com/uniforms-workwear/arc-flash-safety/) (AR garments), can mean the difference between a minor incident and a life-threatening injury.


This guide covers everything you need to know about FR clothing, including flame-resistant[shirts](https://unifirst.com/uniforms-workwear/work-shirts/) , flame-resistant[pants](https://unifirst.com/uniforms-workwear/work-pants/) , and full-body FRC clothes, as well as how to select the right CAT-rated FR/AR gear for maximum protection and OSHA compliance.


## Table of Contents


[OSHA updates](https://unifirst.com/blog/blog-understanding-oshas-new-electric-arc-flash-safety-guidance/) to safety guidance reinforce the vital importance of wearing flame-resistant (FR) clothing, including the appropriate category (CAT 1–4) of FR and arc-rated (AR) garments, when working on or near energized electrical equipment.


Questions and answers every employer and safety manager should know:


- **What are the OSHA requirements for arc flash PPE during energized work?**
OSHA mandates that proper personal protective equipment (PPE), including CAT-rated AR clothing, must be worn for all energized work over 50 volts. Protection ranges from CAT 1 (basic risk) to CAT 4 (severe hazard) depending on the assessed risk level.
- **Do low-voltage tasks still require AR garments?**
Yes. OSHA explicitly clarifies that low-voltage tasks (such as 120–208 volts) still present significant arc flash hazards. These tasks frequently require CAT 1 or CAT 2 AR garments to prevent catastrophic injury.
- **Is AR clothing required if lockout/tagout (LOTO) protocols are already in place?**
Yes. While LOTO procedures are mandatory, de-energizing equipment alone does not completely remove electrical hazards. Wearing compliant AR clothing at the appropriate CAT level during these tasks is strongly recommended to safeguard against residual electrical risks.
- **What are common safety misconceptions regarding arc flash risks?** A common myth is that de-energized systems or low-voltage equipment carry minimal risk. In reality, improperly handled de-energized equipment and low-voltage systems are leading contributors to workplace injuries, underscoring the necessity of CAT-rated arc flash protection in these scenarios.


These standards reflect a proactive shift in workplace safety, addressing emerging risks and strengthening protections for both seasoned electricians and workers new to high-risk electrical environments.


## What is FR clothing and why does it matter?


FR clothing refers to garments specifically designed to resist ignition, self-extinguish within seconds of flame exposure, and minimize injuries caused by burns or molten metal. Unlike standard fabrics, which can ignite and continue burning, FR materials create a protective barrier that significantly reduces the severity of burn injuries.


A core subcategory of FR clothing is[AR garments](https://unifirst.com/uniforms-workwear/arc-flash-safety/) . These are assigned a Category Rating (CAT 1–4) based on their Arc Thermal Performance Value (ATPV) Breakopen Threshold Energy (Ebt), providing precise protection from arc flash hazards. While all AR garments are flame-resistant, not all FR garments are arc-rated, making it critical to understand your specific site risks.


FR and AR clothing, including CAT 1–4 FR garments, are essential across industries like utilities, construction,[oil and gas](https://unifirst.com/blog/prioritizing-safety-through-flame-resistant-uniforms-in-the-oil-and-gas-industry/) , and[manufacturing](https://unifirst.com/industry/manufacturing/) —anywhere sparks, flames, and electrical arcs are regular occupational risks. Beyond protecting lives, FR clothing ensures compliance with strict industry standards:


- **NFPA 70E** – Standard for electrical safety in the workplace (which defines the CAT 1–4 boundaries)
- **NFPA 2112** – Standard on flame-resistant clothing for protection of industrial personnel against short-duration thermal exposures from fire.


[Investing in high-quality flame-resistant shirts](https://unifirst.com/case-study/oil-and-gas-company-improves-productivity-and-reduces-costs-by-10k-with-unifirst/) ,[flame-resistant pants](https://unifirst.com/products/armorex-fr-88-12-flame-resistant-work-pants/) ,[jackets](https://unifirst.com/products/bulwark-fr-flame-resistant-team-jackets/) , and[comprehensive FRC (flame-resistant clothing)](https://unifirst.com/uniforms-workwear/flame-resistant/) solutions with the right CAT level for the role gives workers the confidence to perform dangerous tasks safely, while keeping your business compliant.


## Critical FR clothing items


To help protect your workers, you need the right combination of CAT-rated FR garments. Each type serves a critical function, from daily wear to full-body protection for extreme environments. Always match your CAT 1, CAT 2, CAT 3, or CAT 4 garment selection to your jobsite’s calculated hazard level.


##### FLAME-RESISTANT SHIRTS


[Flame-resistant shirts](https://unifirst.com/uniforms-workwear/all-products/?filter&filter_cat=294&sort_by=featured&product_cats=93%2C98&style=3855&brand=131) are the first line of defense for your upper body. Made from materials like Nomex® or specialized treated cotton, these shirts provide both comfort and protection. Look for shirts featuring:


- ARC RATING


Ensure shirts meet the ATPV appropriate for their intended CAT rating (from CAT 1 minimum to CAT 4 heavy-duty exposure).
- **MOISTURE-WICKING FABRICS** Keeps workers cool, comfortable, and focused during long shifts.
- REINFORCED SEAMS


Designed to withstand rugged daily work environments.
- CAT APPLICATION


CAT 1 and CAT 2 FR shirts are commonly used in general industry and utility work; CAT 3 and CAT 4 shirts are required for severe arc flash risks.


##### FLAME-RESISTANT PANTS


[Flame-resistant pants](https://unifirst.com/uniforms-workwear/all-products/?filter&filter_cat=294&sort_by=featured&product_cats=93%2C97&brand=131) provide critical protection from sparks and molten materials. When selecting pants, consider:


- HIGH-QUALITY FABRICS


Heavy-duty materials like premium denim or canvas blends provide long-lasting wear.
- REINFORCED KNEES


Ideal for tasks that involve kneeling, crawling, or heavy lifting.
- COMFORT FIT


Flexibility and breathability to support all-day productivity.


##### FRC CLOTHING FOR FULL-BODY PROTECTION


For high-risk environments, full body[FR clothing](https://unifirst.com/uniforms-workwear/flame-resistant/) , including coveralls, jackets, and outerwear, provide comprehensive, full-body protection for workers who face significant fire and arc flash hazards. Full-body FR clothing helps ensure that no part of the body is left vulnerable to sparks, flames, or molten debris. Look for features like:


- ARC-RATED SPECIFICATIONS


Choose gear with a CAT rating that matches your highest identified workplace hazard, from CAT 1 for everyday risks up to CAT 4 for the most hazardous environments.
- WEATHER RESISTANCE


Insulated or waterproof FR clothing for extreme conditions.
- FREEDOM OF MOVEMENT


Reinforced seams and ergonomic design like action-back to aid in worker comfort.
- FLAME-RESISTANT ZIPPERS AND CLOSURES


Non-conductive, fabric-covered closures ensure all parts of the garment maintain fire-resistant properties.
- CAT APPLICATION


Full-body CAT 3 and CAT 4 FR coveralls are required for electrical contractors, industrial maintenance technicians, and utility crews performing tasks with extreme arc flash exposure.


## How to choose the right FR clothing


Safety, comfort, and compliance all start with choosing[the right CAT-level FR clothing](https://unifirst.com/uniforms-workwear/flame-resistant/) for your workplace. Conducting a thorough risk assessment ensures you’re not just compliant but also genuinely safeguarding your people. Here is how to build a successful program:


##### Identify Workplace Hazards


- ARC FLASH RISKS


Workers near energized equipment need AR garments with ATPV and CAT levels suitable for the environment. CAT 2 for most general electrical environments, while CAT 3–4 is required for high-energy switchgear and heavy utility work.
- FLASH FIRE RISKS


NFPA 2112-compliant FR clothing is the standard here. CAT 1 or CAT 2 garments are generally recommended for most oil, gas, and chemical worksites with higher CAT levels or specialized layers utilized as thermal hazards increase.


##### ENSURE STANDARDS COMPLIANCE


[Compliant FR clothing](https://unifirst.com/uniforms-workwear/flame-resistant/) helps protect your workers and shields your business from regulatory penalties. Every garment, whether it’s flame-resistant shirts, flame-resistant pants, or flame-resistant coveralls, should feature clear labeling showing compliance with OSHA, NFPA, and ASTM standards, explicitly displaying the appropriate CAT number and ATPV rating. Check garment labels for:


- NPA 70E –


Electrical safety and arc-flash protection
- NFPA 2112 –


Flash fire protection
- ASTM STANDARDS –


Test methods recognized by OSHA for FR performance


##### PRIORITIZE COMFORT


Workers who are uncomfortable are workers who are distracted. When workers are comfortable in their gear, they can focus on the job, not on adjusting their clothing.


The[best FR clothing](https://unifirst.com/blog/six-actions-to-take-to-stay-compliant-in-warm-weather/) combines protection with ergonomic design and breathability to help workers stay productive. Look for:


- Breathable moisture-wicking fabrics that keep workers dry during long shifts
- Flexible, lightweight materials that allow a full range of motion
- Ergonomic fits that don’t restrict movement, thus supporting focus and efficiency during every shift

### Answers to frequently asked questions


### Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)


What is flame-resistant (FR) clothing and why is it important?


Flame-resistant clothing is made from materials designed to resist ignition and self-extinguish once a thermal heat source is removed. FR clothing helps protect workers from clothing ignition and radiant heat during fire hazards, arc flashes, and molten metal exposure, significantly reducing the risk of severe burn injuries.


What are the key updates in OSHA’s arc-flash guidance?


[OSHA’s guidance](https://unifirst.com/blog/blog-understanding-oshas-new-electric-arc-flash-safety-guidance/) clarifies that all energized work above 50 volts requires proper PPE, which includes matching the garment's protection to the hazard. The updates emphasize that low-voltage work (120–208 volts) still presents significant arc-flash hazards that often require CAT 1 or CAT 2 protection.


How do I know if my FR clothing complies with OSHA regulations?


Check the garment’s label. It must display compliance with recognized safety standards like NFPA 70E (for electrical hazards) or NFPA 2112 (for flash fire), alongside its specific CAT number and ATPV rating. Partnering with an expert uniform service provider like UniFirst ensures your clothing meets all active safety standards.


What types of FR clothing should workers wear for full protection?


Workers should wear a coordinated combination of flame-resistant shirts and flame-resistant pants, or full-body FRC clothes like coveralls and multi-layer outerwear. For high-energy risks, full-body CAT 3 and CAT 4 systems ensure no part of the body is left vulnerable. Additional PPE like FR gloves and headgear further enhance safety. The choice of garments depends on the specific hazards of the job site.


When is FR clothing required on the job?


FR clothing is required when workers are exposed to fire hazards, electrical arcs, or molten metal. OSHA mandates FR clothing for tasks involving energized electrical equipment, de-energization procedures, and any work with potential flash fire hazards. It’s crucial for industries such as construction, utilities, oil and gas, and manufacturing.


How should FR clothing be maintained to ensure effectiveness?


FR clothing must be laundered without contaminants that could compromise its properties. You must avoid chlorine bleach, fabric softeners, and starches, which can act as fuel. Choosing a UniFirst managed uniform rental program helps ensure that laundering, inspection, and compliant FR repairs are handled automatically.


What’s the difference between flame-resistant (FR) and flame-retardant clothing?


Flame-resistant clothing is made from inherently fire-resistant fibers or fabrics engineered at the molecular level to self-extinguish.


Flame-retardant clothing typically refers to standard base fabrics that have received a topical chemical treatment. While both provide protection, inherent flame-resistant materials cannot wash out or wear away over time.


Why do OSHA regulations emphasize low-voltage arc flash risks?


Many workers mistakenly believe low-voltage work (120–208 volts) is safe. However, OSHA stresses that low-voltage systems contribute significantly to arc flash injuries, meaning proper CAT 1 or CAT 2 AR garments remain essential to mitigate these hazards.

Employers can help ensure compliance by conducting regular jobsite hazard assessments, providing properly rated FR clothing, and implementing a managed uniform rental program. This ensures garments are professionally inspected, repaired, and replaced so their CAT-rated integrity is never compromised.
